evidence.claim: The Prince of Wales Island Road System crosses a landscape of fjords, dense forest and steep mountains.
evidence.quote: Fjords, steep-sided and forested mountains, and dense stands of trees characterize the terrain on the island.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s Department of Transportation and Public Facilities presents this scenic byway as a journey through temperate rainforest, Native culture and historical artifacts.
evidence.quote: a temperate rainforest with all its natural beauty and wonder, bountiful wildlife, Native culture and historical artifacts.

evidence.claim: Its description covers 260 miles of mostly paved roads linking island communities, with improved gravel roads reaching shorelines and mountains.
evidence.quote: The byway cover s two hundred sixty miles of mostly paved roads that lead to communities on the island

evidence.claim: The network grew out of logging: roads built for timber companies later improved access for hiking and camping.
evidence.quote: Roads built for the logging companies years ago have enabled better access to different parts of the island for hiking and camping.

evidence.claim: Busier routes between communities were upgraded and paved.
evidence.quote: Prince of Wales island's road system is composed primarily of forest logging roads, with the more heavily traveled routes between island communities upgraded. Many of the roads on the island have been upgraded and paved.

evidence.claim: That expansion had limits. Point Baker and Port Protection chose in 1974 to remain outside the road system.
evidence.quote: Point Baker and Port Protection chose in 1974 not to be connected to the road system.

evidence.claim: For the town sequence here, begin with Hydaburg on Sukkwan Strait, then Klawock on the island’s west coast, and finish at Kasaan on its eastern coast.
evidence.quote: Hydaburg is located on the north shore of Sukkwan Strait

evidence.claim: Each has a totem park.
evidence.quote: Stop at one of the Totem Pole parks in Klawock, Hydaburg and Kasaan.

evidence.claim: Farther north, the byway’s attractions include El Capitan Caves and karst landscapes.
evidence.quote: Visit the northern end of the island to see El Capitan Caves and Karst landscapes.

evidence.claim: Logging roads extend beyond the paved network into the forest.
evidence.quote: Logging roads criss-cross the forest.

evidence.quote: More than 50 miles of improved gravel roads extend along shorelines and into the mountains.

evidence.claim: A reliable water supply determined the location of Hydaburg when three Haida villages consolidated here in 1911.
evidence.quote: Hydaburg was formed in 1911 by consolidation of the three Haida villages on Cordova Bay.

evidence.claim: They were Howkan on Long Island, Sukkwan on Sukkwan Island, and Klinkwan at the mouth of Hunter Bay.
evidence.quote: These villages were Howkan on the west coast of Long Island, Sukkwan at the northern end of Sukkwan Island, across Sukkwan Strait from Hydaburg, and Klinkwan on Prince of Wales Island at the mouth of Hunter Bay.

evidence.claim: The town occupies the north shore of Sukkwan Strait, connected to Cordova Bay through Hetta Inlet.
evidence.quote: Hydaburg is located on the north shore of Sukkwan Strait, which connects to Cordova Bay through Hetta Inlet.

evidence.claim: A totem park is one place to encounter its carved poles.
evidence.quote: Stop at one of the Totem Pole parks in Klawock, Hydaburg and Kasaan.

evidence.claim: Hydaburg is also headquarters of the Hydaburg Cooperative Association, which remains a federally recognized tribe.
evidence.quote: The Hydaburg Cooperative Association remains as the federally recognized tribe

evidence.claim: A reliable water supply determined the location of Hydaburg
evidence.quote: The location was chosen because it had a reliable water supply.

evidence.claim: headquarters of the Hydaburg Cooperative Association
evidence.quote: Hydaburg is the headquartered of the Hydaburg Cooperative Association

evidence.claim: Klawock’s totem park displays 21 poles, including originals and replicas from the old village of Tuxekan.
evidence.quote: A Totem Park has 21 totem poles, one of the largest collections in Alaska: it displays original and replica totems from the old village of Tuxekan.

evidence.claim: The connection reaches back to Tlingit people from Tuxekan who used Klawock as a summer fishing camp.
evidence.quote: Klawock's first settlers were Tlingit who came from the northern winter village of Tuxekan. They used it as a fishing camp for the summer period

evidence.claim: Commercial fish processing followed: a trading post and salmon saltery opened in 1868, then a cannery in 1878.
evidence.quote: In 1868, European Americans opened a trading post and a salmon saltery; some years later, in 1878, a San Francisco firm opened the first cannery in Alaska.

evidence.claim: The city later built a carving shed for pole restoration and commissioned a longhouse, Gaanì Ax Adi, in 1998.
evidence.quote: The city built a carving shed to house the poles during restoration, which can be visited. In 1998 the city commissioned the construction of a Long House (named Gaanì Ax Adi) with a new totem pole.

evidence.claim: Kasaan’s move brought its people closer to mining and cannery work, but the poles followed on another timetable.
evidence.quote: This migration was prompted by the promise of jobs and a school occasioned by development of copper mining and a cannery near the present location.

evidence.claim: In 1938, five historic poles and three replicas were moved to New Kasaan.
evidence.quote: In 1938 five historic and three replica totem poles were moved to New Kasaan.

evidence.claim: During the 1930s, Civilian Conservation Corps crews restored Chief Son-I-Hat’s clan house, relocated or replicated poles, and cut a trail from the town to the park and cemeteries.
evidence.quote: In the 1930s, crews from the Civilian Conservation Corps relocated and/or replicated additional totem poles at the house site, restored the house, constructed a small park, and cut a trail from the center of new Kasaan to the park and adjacent cemeteries.

evidence.claim: Kasaan remains headquarters of the Organized Village of Kasaan, a federally recognized Haida tribe.
evidence.quote: Kasaan is the headquarters of the Organized Village of Kasaan, a federally recognized Alaska Native tribe of Haida people.

evidence.claim: Hollis shows that change in miniature. Active as a mining town from 1900 to about 1915, it was abandoned, then re-established as a logging camp in the 1950s; it now has a ferry terminal.
evidence.quote: Hollis was a boom-and-bust mining town, most active from 1900 to about 1915. Abandoned, it was re-established as a logging camp in the 1950s; it now has a population of about 100, and is the location of a ferry terminal.

evidence.claim: The Tongass National Forest covers most of the island.
evidence.quote: The Tongass National Forest covers most of the island.

evidence.claim: The association was established in 1938, following the extension of the Indian Reorganization Act to Alaska in 1936.
evidence.quote: The Hydaburg Cooperative Association was established in 1938 shortly after the  Indian Reorganization Act was extended to Alaska in 1936

flags: Road totals describe different scopes: DOT gives a 260-mile mostly paved byway, about 200 paved miles and a larger logging network; the island article gives a 310-mile scenic highway. Used DOT’s byway figure.
Material is a branching network with mile values restarting after Kasaan. Retained the Hydaburg–Klawock–Kasaan moment order without inventing a single end-to-end route or turn instructions.

Kasaan relocation chronology conflicts: the town article gives 1893 and chiefly 1902–1904; the tribal article says the 18th century. Omitted precise relocation dates and building origin claims pending community-source verification.
Craig government names differ: DOT uses Craig Community Association; other pages use Craig Tribal Association. Omitted the list of tribal governments.
No tribal-authored source is cached. Cultural history uses the saved secondary accounts; no ceremonial access or carving demonstration is promised.

Dropped the unqualified claim that logging roads are now open to everyone: the cache says many are being decommissioned. Ferry schedule and fuel advice omitted because they are not essential to these moments and the cache contains dated transport information.
